comments.text: I am a 70 year old retired U.S. Army Master Sergeant (E8/1972-1993) and former defense contractor worker bee (2005-2010) who spent much of his career in the cold war. What we currently have in Ukraine is similar to the situation that existed for most of WWI on the west front: a stalemate with small gains won or lost by either side from day-to-day. Ukraine simply does not have enough equipment, forces or resources to take back the land they lost in 2022. On the flip side Russia no longer possesses the conventional forces needed to win the war on their terms as long as NATO nations continue to provide equipment and supplies to Ukraine. As for the lost land, Ukraine must accept the ground reality that the land they have lost to Russia is gone forever, especially the Crimea. The only way that could ever change would be if NATO directly intervenes in the war and fights Russia. If that were to happen, we would quickly move to WWIII and most likely a large nuclear exchange, so realistically I don't see such NATO intervention happening, as the stakes are just too high. The question at this point is how much more destruction and death must occur before both sides finally accept the truth that the current situation on the ground is as good as it going to get, and both sides finally end the war?  While personally I don't like to see Russia end the war with Ukrainian land as their ill-gotten gains, the war with it's ever increasing death and destruction must end before it at some point spirals further out of control and we end up in WWIII.

comments.text:
Zelenskyy is not able to cede Crimea, or any other part of Ukraine to Russia. 
 
Under Ukraine’s current constitution, Crimea cannot be legally ceded to Russia without a very difficult process.

Here’s why:
	•	Territorial Integrity: The Constitution of Ukraine (1996) states clearly in Article 2 that “The territory of Ukraine within its present borders is indivisible and inviolable.” Crimea is internationally recognized as part of Ukraine’s territory, despite Russia’s 2014 annexation.
	•	Amending the Constitution: To legally change the borders of Ukraine (such as ceding Crimea), Article 73 of the Constitution requires an all-Ukrainian referendum — meaning the entire population of Ukraine would have to vote on it, not just Crimea or a government decision alone.
	•	Procedure for Amendments: Constitutional amendments involving territorial issues are also subject to a complex process under Articles 154–159. Any change would need:
	•	A proposal by the President or at least one-third of the Parliament (Verkhovna Rada),
	•	Approval by a constitutional majority (at least 300 out of 450 deputies) in Parliament,
	•	And possibly review by the Constitutional Court to ensure the amendment fits within the framework of constitutional principles.
	•	Practical Reality: Politically and socially, the overwhelming majority of Ukrainian politicians and the public view Crimea as an integral part of Ukraine. Thus, even starting the legal process to cede it would likely be impossible under current conditions.

Summary:
Legally, Ukraine would need a national referendum and constitutional amendment to cede Crimea — both extremely unlikely. As it stands, the Ukrainian Constitution protects the country’s territorial integrity very strongly.

comments.text: The depth of your research is impressive. And you are the only channel showing both the Ukrainian side and the Russian side [that I don't support, just to be clear]. Some feedback about your video format: add more 'silent space', or visual 'breaks', between disconnected footage as it can be hard sometimes to realize that you've jumped to a different action. Also, in reference to 31:30 and as per the Third Geneva Convention of 1949, it is prohibited to "expose POWs to public curiosity". Exposure to public curiosity covers the simple disclosure of images of POWs and recordings of interrogations. Even if POWs appear to make voluntary public statements or willingly participate in the recording of images, disclosure to the public remains unlawful. From 2008 until early 2022, Mariupol was controlled by Ukraine.

In 2014, during the Donbas conflict, pro-Russian separatists briefly seized Mariupol, but Ukraine recaptured it by June 2014. After that, it remained under Ukrainian government control for years.

In February 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine (full-scale invasion).

By March–April 2022, Russia heavily attacked and besieged Mariupol.

Most of Mariupol's destruction — including homes, apartments, hospitals, and theaters — happened during Russia's 2022 siege.

By May 2022, Mariupol was fully captured by Russian forces after brutal fighting (notably around the Azovstal steel plant).

Short answer:

If their house was destroyed by April 2022, it was almost certainly destroyed by Russian forces during the 2022 invasion.

comments.text:
The question is can Ukraine hold on until Russia reaches a critical point at which they've simply expended too much manpower and, more importantly, hardware to not only maintain offensives, but actually sustain combat operations across the whole front? if Russia bleeds itself white trying to overwhelm the Ukranian defenses and ultimately allows Ukraine to gain local superiority that they can exploit then this could flip very quickly. A decisive offensive on a weakened sector that exposes the flanks of similarly weakened adjacent units could cause a collapse. The next question is that should Ukraine arrive at a point where they could generate such a collapse, could they expolit it? The numbers suggest that Russia is near to running on fumes. Moreover given the reticence of Russian commanders to push bad news up the line, the Russian leadership may not be fully aware of the true picture. 

Bottom line though, gotta love the ingenuity and resiliance of the Ukranian people. Western Europe needs to look after these people, they're going to make great allies. Whilst waiting for NATO, unilateral alliances between the UK, Norway, and the EU should be on the table.

replies.text:
A Soviet army is marching through a Finnish forest when a general hears a voice from over a hill shout: "one Finnish soldier is better than 10 Soviet soldiers!"

The general promptly send 10 soldiers to root out the voice, there is gunfire, and then silence.

After a few minutes, the voice shouts defiantly: "One Finnish soldier is better than a hundred Soviet soldiers!!"

The general sends a hundred men to remove the nuisance, there is a racket of gunfire, and then quiet.

The voice cries out loudly once more: "One Finnish soldier is better than a thousand Soviet soldiers!!"

Enraged, the general sends a thousand men charging over the hilltop to shut up that voice once and for all, an epic battle rages, and then quiet. After a few minutes, a gravely wounded Soviet crawls back over the hill and cries:

"It's a trap! There are two Finnish soldiers!!"

​@@CatCap409 Russia didn't annex Lugansk and Donetsk before the invasion. It recognized them as independent states. comments.text:
Funny how this video skips key battles like Severodonetsk, Avdiivka— all clear Russian victories in fully committed engagements. Why leave them out? Because it would ruin the illusion of a "balanced" war narrative.

Every time Russia went all-in — Mariupol, Severodonetsk, Bakhmut, Avdiivka, now Kursk — Ukraine fought fiercely, yes, but still lost ground. Meanwhile, Ukraine’s "wins" like Kharkiv or Hostomel happened when Russia chose not to commit or even withdrew strategically.

Tactics matter, but logistics, depth, and attrition win wars. Russia uses artillery and drones not because it's "barbaric", but because it's smart and effective. This isn’t a Hollywood script — it’s a war of endurance. And so far, Russia wins every time it chooses to stay and finish the job.

To this day, Ukrainians have fought with extreme determination, especially in urban warfare.
However, in every battle where Russia fully committed its forces and followed through,
Russia ultimately emerged victorious — often at high cost, but with ground gained.

⚔ Battle Summaries
1. Kiev (Feb–Apr 2022)

Russia launched an assault but never fully committed to siege or urban warfare.

Withdrew under logistical strain and in light of Istanbul peace talks.

No full commitment — Ukrainian defensive success.

2. Kharkiv (Feb–Sep 2022)

Russia occupied areas around Kharkiv but avoided full urban battle.

Ukrainian counteroffensive reclaimed territory; Russian troops withdrew without fight.

No committed battle — Ukrainian gain by maneuver.

3. Mariupol (Feb–May 2022)

Full Russian commitment with siege tactics; total encirclement.

Ukrainians (especially Azov) resisted heroically for months.

Result: Russian victory. City was taken after brutal fighting.

4. Severodonetsk (May–Jun 2022)

Russia committed to grinding urban battle, block-by-block assault.

Ukrainians fought hard but made a tactical withdrawal.

Result: Russian victory.

5. Bakhmut (Aug 2022–May 2023)

Months-long meat-grinder; Ukrainians fought fiercely, trench by trench.

Wagner-led Russian forces fully committed and took the city.

Result: Russian victory. Most symbolic and bloody fight.

6. Avdiivka (Late 2023–Feb 2024)

Russia launched major offensive with full artillery, drone, and infantry use.

Ukraine resisted over months but finally withdrew to avoid encirclement.

Result: Russian victory.
Conclusion:
Ukraine: unmatched bravery, held key symbolic ground early on.

Russia: won every major battle where it chose to fully commit and endure.

These victories, though costly, show Russian superiority in protracted ground engagements — once it decides to finish what it starts.

Russia already lost because 1) Finland and Sweden joined NATO, 2) The eastern block countries gave their old Soviet era weapon systems to Ukraine and replaced them with newer, better, western systems, 3) NATO countries significantly increased their military budgets, 4) Europe has significantly decreased their dependance on Russian fossil fuels and are unlikely to return to using Russian fossil fuels even after the war is ended, 5) Russia has burned through a significant portion of their stockpile of Soviet era weapons, weapons they are unlikely to be able to replace in full even in decades, 6) Russia has shown that their new weapon systems are vastly inferior to western weapon systems. Look to India taking over most of the foreign weapon system sales that Russia used to have. It is sad that Trump wants to end this war when, yes, Ukraine is getting depleted, but Russia is running out of their Soviet stockpile of equipment.  80% of Russian replacement equipment is refurbished Soviet era equipment, which is getting older and older by the quarter (the other 20% is new production).  When they run out of that Soviet stockpile they will have only 1/5th the replacement equipment they have now, and the other 4/5th today is of increasingly poorer quality.  So stopping now makes no sense, when Ukraine can be restocked with new western weapons effectively forever so long as they manage to have the men to use them.  (Russia's economy is half that of Germany, so the west can dedicate a much smaller amount of its economy to military production and still massively outproduce Russia).

comments.text:
Ukraine’s War Was Always Unwinnable: The Nuclear Reality That Western Leaders Ignored

From the moment the war in Ukraine began, one fundamental truth was clear—Ukraine could never achieve a military victory over Russia. This was not a question of willpower or Western support but a basic reality of power dynamics, military capacity, and nuclear deterrence.

Yet, Western leaders deliberately ignored this reality, pushing Ukraine into a war that could only end in devastation. Now, as Ukraine’s losses mount, and NATO’s strategy collapses, it is time to confront a hard but essential truth: this war was never winnable, and the West knew it all along.

1. Russia Views NATO Expansion as an Existential Threat

The foundation of this conflict is simple: Russia has always considered NATO’s expansion—especially into Ukraine and Georgia—to be an existential threat.
 • This is not a debatable issue—it has been stated openly by every major Russian leader since the 1990s, including Gorbachev, Yeltsin, and Putin.
 • In December 2021, just two months before the war began, Russia formally asked the U.S. and NATO for written security guarantees, including a pledge that Ukraine would not join NATO.
 • The West flatly rejected these requests, forcing Russia into a position where military action was the only remaining option to stop NATO’s expansion.

Why does this matter? Because when a nuclear power sees something as an existential threat, it is willing to escalate to the highest level to defend itself.

2. Ukraine Could Never Win—And the West Knew It

A. The Conventional Military Reality
 • Ukraine, even with Western support, could never match Russia’s industrial base, military reserves, and strategic depth.
 • Russia outguns Ukraine in every category: artillery, tanks, air power, electronic warfare, and logistics.
 • Even after receiving billions in NATO weapons, Ukraine’s counteroffensive in 2023 failed miserably, proving that no amount of Western aid could change the battlefield reality.

B. The Nuclear Reality: Russia’s Ultimate Deterrent

Even if Ukraine had been more successful on the battlefield, Russia would never allow itself to be completely defeated.
 • Russia has the world’s largest nuclear arsenal. Its military doctrine allows for first use of nuclear weapons in situations where the existence of the Russian state is at risk.
 • If NATO had directly intervened, or if Ukraine had pushed too far into Russian-held territory, Russia could have escalated with tactical nuclear weapons.
 • A single nuclear strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure or military command centers would have ended the war instantly—just as the U.S. ended Japan’s resistance in 1945 by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

If Ukraine was never in a position to win conventionally, and if Russia had the means to end the war at any moment through escalation, then why did the West push Ukraine into this war in the first place?

3. The West’s Gamble: Pretending Nuclear Reality Didn’t Exist

Instead of acknowledging the basic military and nuclear realities, the U.S. and NATO lied to Ukraine and the world, pushing a strategy that was doomed from the start.
 • They encouraged Ukraine to fight, knowing full well that Ukraine could not win.
 • They rejected Russia’s 2021 security proposals, despite knowing that this would force Russia to act militarily.
 • They ignored decades of warnings from top Western strategists, including George Kennan, Henry Kissinger, and William Burns (now the CIA Director), all of whom predicted that NATO expansion into Ukraine would trigger a war.

This was not a miscalculation—it was a reckless gamble.

Western leaders hoped that:
 1. Russia would collapse internally. (It didn’t.)
 2. Sanctions would destroy Russia’s economy. (They backfired.)
 3. Ukraine’s military, armed with Western weapons, could achieve a battlefield victory. (It failed.)

Now that all of these assumptions have collapsed, Western leaders refuse to admit their mistakes. Instead, they push for more weapons, more escalation, and more Ukrainian sacrifice—even though the end result is inevitable: Russia will not lose.

4. The Hiroshima Parallel: How the War Could Have Ended Quickly

In August 1945, the U.S. ended World War II by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The reasoning was brutal but simple:
 • Japan was not willing to surrender.
 • A full-scale U.S. invasion would have cost millions of lives.
 • The atomic bomb ended the war instantly.

If Russia had been backed into a corner in Ukraine, it could have done the same. A single nuclear strike on Kyiv or key infrastructure targets would have ended Ukraine’s resistance, forcing immediate surrender.

This is not speculation—it is exactly how major wars have ended before, and it is why the West should have never encouraged a military conflict with a nuclear power in the first place.

5. A Frozen Conflict: A War That Never Truly Ends?

Even if the war officially “ends” through a negotiated settlement, there is a high risk that this will become a frozen conflict—where active fighting stops, but the core tensions remain unresolved.
 • Russia is unlikely to fully withdraw from occupied territories, and Ukraine will remain heavily militarized with Western support.
 • This means that the war could reignite at any time, making it an ongoing geopolitical flashpoint.
 • As long as NATO expansion remains an unresolved issue, Russia will continue to view Ukraine as a potential threat, keeping the conflict on standby.

This is why a truly lasting peace would require serious diplomatic engagement, security guarantees, and mutual concessions—something that Western leaders have refused to consider until now. If they continue down this path, they will not be ending the war, only delaying its next phase.

Mearsheimer has warned that this conflict could flare up again anytime. As long as both sides remain heavily armed and the core grievances remain unresolved, Europe will continue living under the shadow of a war that could return at any moment.

6. The Harsh Truth: This War Was Always Going to End in a Negotiated Settlement

Now that Ukraine is running out of men, weapons, and Western support, the only path forward is negotiation. But the brutal irony is that:
 • Ukraine could have had a better deal in 2022, before losing hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
 • Western leaders actively blocked peace talks, forcing Ukraine to keep fighting.
 • Now, as Ukraine’s position deteriorates, the eventual peace deal will be worse than what was possible earlier.

So what was the point of all this destruction?

The West’s strategy has failed, and Ukraine is the one paying the price.

Conclusion: A War That Should Have Never Happened

Ukraine never had a chance to win this war—and every Western leader who pushed for escalation knew it.

The real question is: Why did they push Ukraine into this war anyway?
 • Was it to weaken Russia at Ukraine’s expense?
 • Was it to secure profits for the arms industry?
 • Was it because Western elites refuse to admit when they are wrong?

Whatever the reason, the reality is clear: Ukraine was sacrificed for a Western geopolitical fantasy that was never achievable.

Now, with its army depleted, its economy shattered, and its land in ruins, Ukraine will be forced to accept the same negotiated settlement that could have been reached two years ago—except now, on far worse terms.

If Western leaders had been honest from the start, this war could have been avoided. Instead, they chose escalation over diplomacy—and Ukraine has paid the ultimate price.

comments.text:
Ukraine’s War Was Always Unwinnable: The Nuclear Reality That Western Leaders Ignored

From the moment the war in Ukraine began, one fundamental truth was clear—Ukraine could never achieve a military victory over Russia. This was not a question of willpower or Western support but a basic reality of power dynamics, military capacity, and nuclear deterrence.

Yet, Western leaders deliberately ignored this reality, pushing Ukraine into a war that could only end in devastation. Now, as Ukraine’s losses mount, and NATO’s strategy collapses, it is time to confront a hard but essential truth: this war was never winnable, and the West knew it all along.

1. Russia Views NATO Expansion as an Existential Threat

The foundation of this conflict is simple: Russia has always considered NATO’s expansion—especially into Ukraine and Georgia—to be an existential threat.
 • This is not a debatable issue—it has been stated openly by every major Russian leader since the 1990s, including Gorbachev, Yeltsin, and Putin.
 • In December 2021, just two months before the war began, Russia formally asked the U.S. and NATO for written security guarantees, including a pledge that Ukraine would not join NATO.
 • The West flatly rejected these requests, forcing Russia into a position where military action was the only remaining option to stop NATO’s expansion.

Why does this matter? Because when a nuclear power sees something as an existential threat, it is willing to escalate to the highest level to defend itself.

2. Ukraine Could Never Win—And the West Knew It

A. The Conventional Military Reality
 • Ukraine, even with Western support, could never match Russia’s industrial base, military reserves, and strategic depth.
 • Russia outguns Ukraine in every category: artillery, tanks, air power, electronic warfare, and logistics.
 • Even after receiving billions in NATO weapons, Ukraine’s counteroffensive in 2023 failed miserably, proving that no amount of Western aid could change the battlefield reality.

B. The Nuclear Reality: Russia’s Ultimate Deterrent

Even if Ukraine had been more successful on the battlefield, Russia would never allow itself to be completely defeated.
 • Russia has the world’s largest nuclear arsenal. Its military doctrine allows for first use of nuclear weapons in situations where the existence of the Russian state is at risk.
 • If NATO had directly intervened, or if Ukraine had pushed too far into Russian-held territory, Russia could have escalated with tactical nuclear weapons.
 • A single nuclear strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure or military command centers would have ended the war instantly—just as the U.S. ended Japan’s resistance in 1945 by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

If Ukraine was never in a position to win conventionally, and if Russia had the means to end the war at any moment through escalation, then why did the West push Ukraine into this war in the first place?

3. The West’s Gamble: Pretending Nuclear Reality Didn’t Exist

Instead of acknowledging the basic military and nuclear realities, the U.S. and NATO lied to Ukraine and the world, pushing a strategy that was doomed from the start.
 • They encouraged Ukraine to fight, knowing full well that Ukraine could not win.
 • They rejected Russia’s 2021 security proposals, despite knowing that this would force Russia to act militarily.
 • They ignored decades of warnings from top Western strategists, including George Kennan, Henry Kissinger, and William Burns (now the CIA Director), all of whom predicted that NATO expansion into Ukraine would trigger a war.

This was not a miscalculation—it was a reckless gamble.

Western leaders hoped that:
 1. Russia would collapse internally. (It didn’t.)
 2. Sanctions would destroy Russia’s economy. (They backfired.)
 3. Ukraine’s military, armed with Western weapons, could achieve a battlefield victory. (It failed.)

Now that all of these assumptions have collapsed, Western leaders refuse to admit their mistakes. Instead, they push for more weapons, more escalation, and more Ukrainian sacrifice—even though the end result is inevitable: Russia will not lose.

4. The Hiroshima Parallel: How the War Could Have Ended Quickly

In August 1945, the U.S. ended World War II by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The reasoning was brutal but simple:
 • Japan was not willing to surrender.
 • A full-scale U.S. invasion would have cost millions of lives.
 • The atomic bomb ended the war instantly.

If Russia had been backed into a corner in Ukraine, it could have done the same. A single nuclear strike on Kyiv or key infrastructure targets would have ended Ukraine’s resistance, forcing immediate surrender.

This is not speculation—it is exactly how major wars have ended before, and it is why the West should have never encouraged a military conflict with a nuclear power in the first place.

5. A Frozen Conflict: A War That Never Truly Ends?

Even if the war officially “ends” through a negotiated settlement, there is a high risk that this will become a frozen conflict—where active fighting stops, but the core tensions remain unresolved.
 • Russia is unlikely to fully withdraw from occupied territories, and Ukraine will remain heavily militarized with Western support.
 • This means that the war could reignite at any time, making it an ongoing geopolitical flashpoint.
 • As long as NATO expansion remains an unresolved issue, Russia will continue to view Ukraine as a potential threat, keeping the conflict on standby.

This is why a truly lasting peace would require serious diplomatic engagement, security guarantees, and mutual concessions—something that Western leaders have refused to consider until now. If they continue down this path, they will not be ending the war, only delaying its next phase.

Mearsheimer has warned that this conflict could flare up again anytime. As long as both sides remain heavily armed and the core grievances remain unresolved, Europe will continue living under the shadow of a war that could return at any moment.

6. The Harsh Truth: This War Was Always Going to End in a Negotiated Settlement

Now that Ukraine is running out of men, weapons, and Western support, the only path forward is negotiation. But the brutal irony is that:
 • Ukraine could have had a better deal in 2022, before losing hundreds of thousands of soldiers.
 • Western leaders actively blocked peace talks, forcing Ukraine to keep fighting.
 • Now, as Ukraine’s position deteriorates, the eventual peace deal will be worse than what was possible earlier.

So what was the point of all this destruction?

The West’s strategy has failed, and Ukraine is the one paying the price.

Conclusion: A War That Should Have Never Happened

Ukraine never had a chance to win this war—and every Western leader who pushed for escalation knew it.

The real question is: Why did they push Ukraine into this war anyway?
 • Was it to weaken Russia at Ukraine’s expense?
 • Was it to secure profits for the arms industry?
 • Was it because Western elites refuse to admit when they are wrong?

Whatever the reason, the reality is clear: Ukraine was sacrificed for a Western geopolitical fantasy that was never achievable.

Now, with its army depleted, its economy shattered, and its land in ruins, Ukraine will be forced to accept the same negotiated settlement that could have been reached two years ago—except now, on far worse terms.

If Western leaders had been honest from the start, this war could have been avoided. Instead, they chose escalation over diplomacy—and Ukraine has paid the ultimate price.

comments.author: @grahamlait1969
comments.text: The Spartan series of AFVs had to be small and lightweight because it is airmobile. In other words, can be carried in aircraft. The aircraft it was designed to be carried in was the C130 Hercules. The spartan only weighs about ten tonnes, so a Hercules could carry two of them. The idea was to provide some armour for airmobile forces but it had to sacrifice armoured protection, which is, of course, heavy, and to substitute protection with speed and mobility in a quick deployment. The fact that the Ukrainians can still make good use of it after all this time when they're using it in roles for which it was not primarily designed at all is, of itself, remarkable.

replies.author: @ianjardine7324
replies.text: @@Bravo_Two_Zero  A lot of people make comments about them without knowing what they're talking about. True the armour isn't up to modern western standards but it's about as good a base model  BMP. Almost all maintenance and repairs with the exception of lifting the engine and gearbox can be done with onboard tools even the engine decks can be lifted off by hand it just takes four men and the right coordination. The engine is a standard Cummins diesel so it and the gearbox can be lifted out with any basic vehicle mounted crane or even a good chain hoist. It's not a Bradley a Warrior or a BMP it's never going to go toe to toe with enemy armour because that's not the job it was built for but it is a cheap fast reliable battlefield taxi able to get infantry anti armour or anti air teams into ambush positions quickly and quietly through terrain no other vehicles could. That's why the troop capacity is so small it was never supposed to carry a section of regular infantry it was designed to move small teams of specialists to wherever they were needed most quickly to size and defend critical objectives until slower heavier elements could arrive. Such as airfield's power plants bridges ect. It was designed post WWII when the British forces were drawing down and maintaining large garrison's in all our remaining overseas territories simply wasn't affordable so we switched to a large airmobile rapid response force which could secure a beach head for larger forces to use.

The tracks can also be fitted with spikes that grip ice and snow, so you can still keep going in winter conditions at speed. Operating the GPMG closed down was a bit of a nightmare because the traverse and elevation were manual, not electric, and consequently not quick. The Browning mod sounds like a reasonable, if risky choice. 
You have to be mindful of speed when cornering though - I saw a Spartan lose its track when cornering on the road in Germany, and roll. The radio op dragged the commander down from the turret as they rolled and probably saved his life. 
The electric boiling vessel (BV) was an awesome piece of kit, and the best mod for that was to bin the supplied tap which always leaked, and replace it with a Chieftain fuel tap.

comments.text:
Here’s a simplified breakdown using major transformative wars in U.S. history:

American Revolutionary War – 1775

Civil War – 1861

86 years later

World War II – 1941 (U.S. entry)

80 years after the Civil War started

Present – 2020s

80+ years since WWII began

So yes, there’s a rough pattern of about 80 years between these massive, society-shaping wars.

This idea is the basis of the “Fourth Turning” theory by Strauss and Howe, which suggests American history goes through 80–100 year cycles ending in a major crisis (often a war). Each "turning" is like a generation-long season, and the fourth one is the crisis phase that resets society.

We’re arguably in or near one of those turning points now,

comments.text:
São Paulo (Brazil), March 5, 2023.

Autocracies and dictatorships are dumb systems with no legitimacy.

According to Peter Drucker, being efficient is doing things right (doing things correctly); and being effective is doing the right things (doing those things that lead to the achievement of desired goals).

For example, we are being efficient and effective when we drive correctly on the right road that will take us to the desired destination.

And how can we know, moment by moment, whether we are being efficient and effective? Very simple: examining, at every moment, the feedback we receive. In the case of the road, the feedback groups are the signals along the road and the signals that the instruments in our car give us.

Our intelligence, as individuals and as a species, is directly proportional to our ability to be efficient and effective in solving the problems that afflict us.

Dictatorial and autocratic governments not only ignore feedback but prohibit citizens from providing it, punishing those who dare to do so. Therefore, they are dumb systems, causing serious problems, as history has shown.

And precisely because they are dumb systems that impose themselves on citizens to exploit these citizens, autocracies and dictatorships have no legitimacy.

And they get to be vampiric: the Putin regime, in order to maintain itself, continually needs the blood of the young people it throws into the carnage of war.

Prof. Alvaro C. G. Gemignani

Я из Казани. Как же мне больно и стыдно за свою страну, и за ее народонаселение (до граждан еще не доросли). Огромное разочарование. Бестолковые, раболепные, инфантильные (авторитарная инфантилизация) имперцы. Гос шовинизм и бытовая ксенофобия - наше (точнее, их) - все! 
Делаю, что могу. Угрозы везде. Даже в комментах не ютубе. Даже не этом канале уже грозили прийти за мной. Нас, тех, кто все понимает - около 20% (ну, насколько вообще возможно провести подсчеты ). Среди молодежи конечно больше думающих, среди бумеров в основном постсовковый менталитет. Мы с сестрой перестали общаться с родителями.  Они начали втирать, что нужно рожать солдат (у меня 2 дочки). Зомби! 
Чувствуем свою вину. Хотя, я выходила на все митинги. Убигали от полиции... 
Как же больно! 
Бессилие, разочарование.

Stationed is okay, based would be preferred.  We understand your intent but there is a technical difference.

 In USAF parlance a "base" has an airfield and airplanes, like Ramstein Air Force Base.  A "station" has USAF personnel and equipment but no airplanes, like Hessisch-Oldendorf Air Force Station. 

Using stationed rather than based would only matter to a small group of people that would insist on very strict adherence to maybe overly specific details.

replies.author: @neoprofin
replies.text:
My family (including myself) have served in the Navy, Army, Marines, and NG from WWII to Korea, Vietnam, Somalia, Iraq.

I married a German girl I met while backpacking, I exported her to the US and we got her citizenship and have a beautiful angelic child together.

But yes, at some point I had to ask the uncomfortable question of what her grandfather did during the war. He was a Lutheran pastor and when things got bleak he was told serve or go to jail. He just drove a supply truck and *very illegally* took hundreds of photos from basic training to his time on the front lines. It all reminded me of my time in service. It's not Steven Segal mayhem, it's taking a moment of peace to eat some chow, or finding a cute cat to play with. Some Germans were truly evil, but I refuse to make a blanket statement, every civilization has it's bad actors, and sadly the US is right back at it.

replies.author: @rainerzufall42
replies.text: About that "finally": Don't you think, there are reasons for our precautious approach? For almost 50 years, we were occupied because the other countries feared us. The situation was similar to the Ukraine situation now, we were the buffer to the land of evil. Then there was a period, in which our own constitution didn't allow to wage military force, but we payed most of it, although the reunification was a very expensive (and valuable) thing. At the same time, we were a country surrounded by 9 friendly neighbors, and less money was spent on military. NATO lost some of its purpose, I remember a meeting in 1994, where they looked out for new targets. Our goal was mostly to avoid military conflict by diplomacy. We know that doesn't always work, but you should try it. And that's how we got to this point. There's still a huge part of the population that is quite cautious against military force. With that history (and respecting it, looking to you, US), it's not possible to re-arm in a nonchalant way...

These are different Systems Patriot's range is about 160km while iris-t slm's range is about 40km.
A shot with Patriot costs > 4 Mio USD, while you'll get 10-15 IRIS-T rockets for this money.
An advantage of patriot is that it is capable of intercepting a variety of ballistic missiles, while an Iris-t system ensures near 100% protection from drones, aircrafts, cruise missiles, helicopters etc. with an incredible >98% hit-rate. One IRIS-T system had even a hit-rate above 100%, after downing 2 drones that were flying close together with one missile.

Nice side effect: you can use the IRIS-T missiles as air to air missiles as well.

Dear General Cavoli, I'm aware that beside bombing the living daylight out of innocent civilians in central Europe and getting kicked out of Afghanistan by goat herders on sandals with a Kalashnikov, some improvised explosives and occasionally a handheld rocket launcher, you never achieved a single victory in battle in your whole carrier.

Production of military equipment has surely contributed to the growth of the Russian economy, but the biggest growth was in construction, machine building and appliances.
This growth is the direct result of western sanctions on Russia, which forced the Russians to replace sanctioned goods, previously supplied by the west, with locally produced products.
You're also wrong about the production of military equipment being un-productive.
Why do you think the military industry in the US is so extensive? 
Russia was and still is one of the major suppliers of military equipment in the world and will keep doing so for the foreseeable future.
Most of the Russian companies involved in the production of military equipment are dual use producers and they will have no problem transitioning to the production of civilian good when this conflict will come to an end.
There is a lot of money to be made from military equipment and Russia is surely not going to leave that money on the table for their competitors to grab it.
Russians think that they should send a thank you letter to the west for imposing these sanctions, because they boosted their economy and demonstrated that Russia can very well do without western supplied goods. Russia is now virtually completely self sufficient and the few products they can't produce up to now, can easily be obtained from their allies.
Inflation in Russia is high, but not out of the ordinary. 
Furthermore, this inflation is not due to the ramping up of military production, but due to out of control investment in construction and the fact that incomes in Russia are rising, giving the population more money to spend. The growth was so strong that it caused a shortage of manpower in Russia's economy.
The Russian national bank recognized these problems and increase interest rates dramatically to get this spending and inflation back under control and prevent the economy from overheating. 
As far as I can see, they are successful in doing so. The manpower shortage is getting better and inflation is poised to normalize in the coming months.
The territory in Kursk held by Ukraine, that you call sizable, needs to be found on the map with a magnifying glass and consist out of a few settlements, not even a towns, but rather some clusters of houses and farms, which don't hold any strategic value and is shrinking every single day. This whole operation was a complete disaster which came at the cost of the lives of thousands of Ukraine's best trained and most experienced soldiers and hundreds of pieces of heavy equipment and armor. 
The Belgorod incursion will not fare any better and is merely intended to divert the attention away from the Ukrainian failures all over the 2000 Km front lines.
The Russian offensive in the Bachmut area is not petered out, but merely paused due to the weather conditions, which make it difficult to operate heavy armor and other equipment. 
Anyone who followed this conflict knows that this is happening every year during this period and it amazes me that an officer of your rank doesn't seem to know this.
Currently the Russians already restarted the fighting in this area and they are making significant progress every single day. The little progress the Ukrainians made during the previous period is already lost and the Russians are taking ever more territory along the whole line of contact every single day.
Ukraine is still able to concentrate a good portion of it's military in an area where the Russian defenses are the weakest and make some progress, but after a few days or weeks they are driven back by the Russians and lose even more territory.

Now, Putin doesn't even have 100 operable modern tanks, perhaps he has none. The tank marshalling yards and staging areas no longer show any Russian tanks! I'm old and this is the most dangerous time for WWIII in my lifetime.

replies.text: Right.  This is something I've been waiting for.  Russia's Soviet stockpiles are mostly depleted-- not entirely.  It seems like they are able to build new missiles and Iran helped them build factories for Shehed drones.  However, they don't seem able to build much else in terms of military hardware.  Even the new Su35s are said to have very low build quality and the Armadas never really made it past prototyping and very limited production with all kinds of problems.  Ukraine, however, is producing armored vehicles, drones, and innovative missiles, among many other things (combat lasers, integrated air defense and battle management systems, etc).  Russia still has vast amounts of artillery shells and missiles from  North Korea but Russia's artillery pieces are running low.  Also, Russia has lost a lot of their anti-battery capabilities and air defense capabilities.  The tide could begin to turn again and this time hard against the Russians.  First, we have to see what they do in their Spring offensive.  The Russians method that pushed Ukrainian forces from Kursk was unique and it would be bad if they are able to replicate it.  I heard that, at the same time the U.S. stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine, the Russians also suddenly had numerous precise coordinates of Ukrainian ammo dumps and troop locations.  It wasn't just that the supply road was nearly cut.

@@StarzeGaming Out of oil? No. Petroleum as an industry will decline to the point that it's not worth extracting before they run out. Oil companies are already backing off on exploratory drilling because they really don't think they'll need it and want to save the money for things that consider more important, like paying the shareholders.

But damage to refinery capacity reduces the amount of oil that Russia can take out of the ground. They don't have the storage capacity to just bank it once it's pumped up. It's got to be sold or refined to make room for more. And oil wells do not like having the flow of oil stopped, it's a giant pain in the ass to get it flowing again. So Russia can very easily lose long-term oil extraction capacity.

comments.text:
There is indeed human wave tactics from Russian side, but it has a completely different meaning from implied WW1-2 one: non-stop infantry infiltrations of very small squads (3-5 people at a time) across the whole frontline. No "hooray" charges at all. "Meat" is a focus on humans doing stealth infiltrations, and they are guided by drones to sneak by and the only vehicles they might use are bikes and carts to quickly cross before being spotted by enemy drones.

These tactics were pioneered  by Wagner group first couple years of the war, and after Wagner de-facto dissolution were spread and adopted by whole Russian infantry and naval infantry on the front.

This reminds Terminator movies and when future shown with humans crawling around to avoid enemy machines.

comments.author: @jjohansen86
comments.text:
The vast majority of Americans continue to support Ukraine. We believe that it is the right thing to do. I think it's worth addressing Trump saying that Ukraine has been "taking advantage of" American aid: in one sense, that's true, I don't think that, even in victory, Ukraine is likely to be able to repay America financially, because Russia's brutality has caused billions of dollars worth of damage, and Ukraine will need to worry about rebuilding. However, we knew from the start that this wasn't about getting paid back, it's just the right thing to do. Zelensky's repeated thanks for American aid demonstrate that he understands this, too, that this is just one group of people helping another. And in recent polls, over 70% of Americans still think that this is worth doing, with over half saying that they believe that we should aid for as long as it takes, until Ukraine is restored to pre-invasion borders. With those numbers, it's clear that even those who voted for Trump did so for other reasons. So I want our Ukrainian friends to know... the majority of Americans, we still support you, even if it might not seem like it when you hear Trump.

But I also want to say: Even though we don't expect to be repaid and we want to support Ukraine because it's the right thing to do, many are simply unaware of the other ways that Ukraine is repaying us for our help. Ukrainian soldiers have experience that nobody else in the world has, and they've already begun to pass their knowledge on to NATO countries, including the US. I want to say thank you to Ukraine for this effort. Thank you for helping to train Americans so that they are more prepared in case another war breaks out.

I am so sorry for Trump's betrayal. I understand that he might stop aid again, and no matter how supportive I feel, that doesn't translate into 155 mm artillery shells, I don't have the ability to give the aid that my country's government can. I'll be praying for you, because that's what I can do, and pushing in the tiny way I can to ensure support continues, because I can do that, too.

replies.author: @trevorkrause7220
replies.text: "Decimate" literally means one in ten and was originally used to put down potential revolts in the Roman legions. If any of the military units of the Roman army had shown clear signs of revolt or refusing to obey orders from superior officers but there was little evidence of specific ringleaders the soldiers of that unit were forced to parade as one rank and numbered off. Every tenth man was then taken from the line and executed, often by fellow soldiers in the unit to both prove their new-found loyalty and as a dire warning not to ever be part of a revolt at anytime in the future. It would be up to debate as to whether the loss of ten percent of a military combat strength was a major catastrophe or not. Maybe it could be for the Ukrainian military but also seems a relatively normal and regular occurrence for Russian military combat units who probably expect and sustain much greater losses.

replies.text: @@danielr5637 Oreshnik isnt anything new per se. It's a nuclear capable IRBM (Intermediate Range Ballistic Missile). It follows a ballistic trajectory and can actually quite easily be shot down. The American PAC-3, Aegis, GMD, and THAAD systems are all capable of taking it down, Israel's David's Sling can take it down, The French and Italian Aster 30 Block 1s can also take it down. The part that makes Oreshnik hard to shoot down for Ukraine is that is utilizes a MIRV style payload (Multiple Independent Reentry Vehicle). It also doesn't use a kinetic payload, its designed to use chemical (explosives) or nuclear ones. The interesting thing is that the stated Mach 10 speed of Oreshnik actually puts it as slower than older IRBMs like the American PGM-17 Thor and PGM-19 Jupiter which were retired in 1963.

So you see that everybody can give a hand in some way or other. So gather some energy and/or a little money and start contributing to Ukraines victory!!!!

comments.text:
Just because a signal is encrypted doesnt mean it can't get washed out. It just means its very difficult to high jack it, but with many samples its still very possible, and I thibk Ukraine probably has the highest sample size outside of russia.

Either way to flood the GPS signal only requires a general idea of what frequency is being used and again Ukraine has probably had enough of a sample size for a long time but took a while longer to discover how to use the i formation.

A basic example of how a signal could be flooded and washed out is something everyone is familiar with. A phone camera, under normal conditions a phone can easily compensate for less than ideal white light and balance the color of a picture you are trying to take to make it look as expected rather than slightly blue or yellow depending on lighting. Now flood the scene with green light and the phone wont know what to do and thr outcome will be less than ideal.

comments.text: I don't understand what signal encryption has to do with resistance to jamming. Encryption is a measure to prevent your adversary from using your navigation system. If there is a possibility of spoofing it, then cryptographic signing (authenticating), rather than encrypting (obscuring) is the countermeasure. But ultimately, just good old saturation of receiver circuits with excessively strong signal on frequency (or frequencies) used is sufficient to blind the guidance system.

comments.author: @dichebach
comments.text:
The U.S. does not currently have any systems quite like Archer or Caesar. In fact, the U.S. Army has recognized the need for wheeled self-propelled artillery, which is why it is currently testing the BAE Systems Archer and the French Caesar as potential future acquisitions.

The closest systems in the U.S. arsenal are: HIMARS (High Mobility Artillery Rocket System); M109A7 Paladin (Tracked Self-Propelled Howitzer). However, neither is a true equivalent.

HIMARS offers similar mobility but is well-suited for a different role. HIMARS offers comparable high mobility, but it is far more expensive, logistically demanding, and not suited for the same tactical role as Archer and Caesar. HIMARS excels at striking high-value, distant targets with precision-guided rockets and ballistic missiles, but it lacks the sustained firepower needed for frequent engagements against platoon- or squad-sized elements—a role for which Archer and Caesar are much better suited.


Attempting to use HIMARS in this way would be cost-prohibitive, both in terms of munitions and operational overhead. Not to mention that the cost per launcher and per munition is roughly 10 times higher than traditional 155mm artillery shells.
M109A7 Paladin: Heavily Armored but Less Mobile

The M109A7 Paladin is more similar to Archer and Caesar in terms of function, but it is: More expensive; Heavier and slower; Less mobile in dynamic battlefield conditions; Slower rate of fire. The tracked Paladin is optimized for sustained operations in a high-intensity conflict—the kind of large-scale armor engagements envisioned during the Cold War. It was designed to support heavy mechanized formations in battles between armored brigades, rather than the highly mobile shoot-and-scoot doctrine seen in modern warfare.

Archer and Caesar are superior for the type of modern artillery warfare seen in Ukraine, where:

Mobility and evasion are more important than survivability in direct combat
Firepower needs to be sustained yet cost-effective
Rapid deployment & relocation ("shoot-and-scoot") is critical to avoid counterbattery fire

While the Paladin offers greater armor protection, it is ill-suited for fast-moving, cost-sensitive conflicts where a well-timed artillery barrage followed by immediate relocation is the key to survival. In contrast, Archer and Caesar’s wheeled platforms allow for quick repositioning and lower logistical costs, making them far more practical in modern asymmetrical warfare.

Russia also does not have a direct equivalent to the Archer or Caesar wheeled self-propelled howitzers in terms of mobility, automation, and modern battlefield effectiveness. While Russia fields a variety of self-propelled artillery systems, most are either tracked (like the M109A7 Paladin) or less advanced in automation and mobility than Archer and Caesar.

comments.text: The disaster in Kursk has absolutely nothing to do with the US very short lived military/intelligence aid pause. Then he had a chance in the spring of 2022 to secure a peace with Russia at terms that were immeasurably more favorable compared to what is currently being offered. @@ronallens6204 None of the northern people? Denmark and Norway has been part of Nato for a very long time.

The reason Sweden and Finland has not been part of Nato is because we didn't want to build up unnecessary tension with Russia in the north that would cause a nordic arm race. @@ZoZo-st2ts My apologies, I had responded already but the reply appears to have vanished, so here I go typing this whole essay again! :)

This conversation can definitely take a few hours, but I'll usually start even far before 2008.
I will typically begin with how the US and Russia together defeated Germany in WWII.
How after this, the Cold war began, leading up to the collapse of the Soviet Union, and the Budapest Memorandum, where Russia, the US and UK lobbied to disarm countries from their nuclear weapons with the promise of protection.
I will run them through the various presidents Russia has had since then, and how Russia and the West have interacted since then.
I'll talk about the multiple annexations and invasions that Russia has conducted, such as during the second Chechen war and the invasion of Georgia.
Then comes the Revolution of Dignity, in Ukraine, where the Pro-Russian president was ousted by Ukrainian rebellion, immediately followed by Russia's annexation of Crimea.
I walk them through the Minsk Agreements and how the West responded to Russia's occupation of Crimea, including the reactions of president Obama and eventually Donald Trump, who provided some military aid but then also blackmailed Ukraine by withholding said aid which resulted in his first impeachment.
Then of course, the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia.
I cover how the frontline has developed over the years, and where Ukraine's support has mostly come from and what the real numbers are, backed up with various sources across the whole political spectrum.
Then, leading up to the last weeks, I show them the footage (The full footage!) of meetings such as the Oval Office meeting between Vance, Trump and Zelensky, and explain the terms both Russia and Ukraine are trying to set for a ceasefire, including why Zelensky is pushing for security guarantees.
At this point, the Republicans I talk to will often already realize by themselves that Trump has a highly simplistic and skewed view of this war, and why Zelensky brought up the points that he did during this meeting.
I have frequently heard reactions along the lines of "Wait, but then Russia will just invade again later!", I don't need to explain this to them by then.
Then I explain the way in which Trump is pressuring Ukraine, and not Russia, into agreeing with said ceasefire which would leave them highly vulnerable in the future.

Most importantly, we have to explain the full story. That means both acknowledging that there has been corruption in the Ukrainian army, but also that they have taken major steps to fix this with good results.
That means explaining the good Trump has done for Ukraine, such as providing some military aid throughout his first term, but also his attempt to blackmail Ukraine, or sabotage aid packages for Ukraine's 2023 spring counter-offensive.
I won't blame them for voting for Trump, I know fully well why many of them have, but once they know the full story of situations like these, and what trump is doing to the US, they do change their mind.

Finally, I will tell them not to blindly trust even my own information, because no one person can be trusted to know everything. I will ask them to do the research for themselves, and I believe that when they do, they will see with their own eyes what we tell them.
I hope this answers your question!

comments.author: @RalphBrooker-gn9iv
comments.text:
Ex-Brit infantryman here 1978-1990). In my day trenches were deep, revetted, deturfed and isolated (no trench network as in WWI and in Ukraine). They were defence oriented and armour resistant (you’d be safe if a tank rolled over your position). I’ve followed this war wishing our Ukrainian brothers-in-arms all the best, whilst realising that the role of the trench has changed and that Ukrainian troops will soon be teaching us. The quick alternative to our old well-constructed, defensive fire-trenches were shell-scrapes; rapidly and easily constructed, whilst the fire trench was such a technical ‘thing of beauty’ it sometimes needed help from sappers (eg, getting the depth with diggers). Those days were also intended for a Russian armoured assault. 
Slava Ukraine 🇺🇦

comments.text:
Former President of Poland Lech Walesa wrote the following letter to Trump.
Your Excellency, Mr. President,
We watched the report of your conversation with the President of Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelensky, with fear and distaste. We find it insulting that you expect Ukraine to show respect and gratitude for the material assistance provided by the United States in its fight against russia. Gratitude is owed to the heroic Ukrainian soldiers who shed their blood in defense of the values of the free world. They have been dying on the front lines for more than 11 years in the name of these values and the independence of their homeland, which was attacked by Putin’s russia.
We do not understand how the leader of a country that symbolizes the free world cannot recognize this.
Our alarm was also heightened by the atmosphere in the Oval Office during this conversation, which reminded us of the interrogations we endured at the hands of the Security Services and the debates in Communist courts. Prosecutors and judges, acting on behalf of the all-powerful communist political police, would explain to us that they held all the power while we held none. They demanded that we cease our activities, arguing that thousands of innocent people suffered because of us. They stripped us of our freedoms and civil rights because we refused to cooperate with the government or express gratitude for our oppression. We are shocked that President Volodymyr Zelensky was treated in the same manner.
The history of the 20th century shows that whenever the United States sought to distance itself from democratic values and its European allies, it ultimately became a threat to itself. President Woodrow Wilson understood this when he decided in 1917 that the United States must join World War I. President Franklin Delano Roosevelt understood this when, after the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941, he resolved that the war to defend America must be fought not only in the Pacific but also in Europe, in alliance with the nations under attack by the Third Reich.
We remember that without President Ronald Reagan and America’s financial commitment, the collapse of the Soviet empire would not have been possible. President Reagan recognized that millions of enslaved people suffered in Soviet russia and the countries it had subjugated, including thousands of political prisoners who paid for their defense of democratic values with their freedom. His greatness lay, among other things, in his unwavering decision to call the USSR an “Empire of Evil” and to fight it decisively. We won, and today, the statue of President Ronald Reagan stands in Warsaw, facing the U.S. Embassy.
Mr. President, material aid—military and financial—can never be equated with the blood shed in the name of Ukraine’s independence and the freedom of Europe and the entire free world. Human life is priceless; its value cannot be measured in money. Gratitude is due to those who sacrifice their blood and their freedom. This is self-evident to us, the people of Solidarity, former political prisoners of the communist regime under Soviet russia.
We call on the United States to uphold the guarantees made alongside Great Britain in the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which established a direct obligation to defend Ukraine’s territorial integrity in exchange for its relinquishment of nuclear weapons. These guarantees are unconditional—there is no mention of treating such assistance as an economic transaction.
Signed,
Lech Wałęsa, former political prisoner, President of Poland

As a progressive American patriot from southern Indiana, my steadfast support for Ukraine in its valiant struggle against Russia’s barbaric incursion has been resolute from the outset. Ukraine is a sovereign democracy, a nation unequivocally entitled to exist in tranquility, free from foreign despotism. The entire rules-based international order must rally behind Ukraine, not merely as an ethical obligation, but as an imperative for global stability and the preservation of democratic ideals.

Russia’s invasion transcends mere military aggression—it is grand larceny on an imperial scale. Beyond its insatiable territorial ambitions, the Kremlin seeks to expropriate Ukraine’s abundant resources: its vast mineral wealth, oil fields, agricultural output, and strategic Black Sea ports. This war is not about “security concerns” or “historical ties”; it is outright pillaging. No principled nation should remain idle while a fascist autocracy plunders and subjugates a peaceful democracy.

As an American, the righteousness of Ukraine’s struggle is self-evident. I perceive it thus: if a violent criminal cabal besieged my neighbor’s home—murdering loved ones, committing atrocities, abducting children, and occupying rooms—would I stand idle? Absolutely not. I would stand in solidarity, repel the intruders, and demand justice. The only difference is that this is not a solitary household—it is an entire nation.

Yet today, a segment of American voters has elevated our own authoritarian demagogue, a man who brazenly venerates the malefactor in this tragedy. Donald Trump’s ignoble reverence for Putin is a flagrant betrayal of every American who has ever opposed tyranny. He desecrates the legacy of those who vanquished fascism. No true patriot should abide such cowardice and perfidy.

Growing up in the Midwest, I was instilled with an abiding contempt for bullies. Putin is one of the greatest oppressors today—a despotic oligarch determined to extinguish democracy wherever it flourishes. America must remain unwavering. We must fortify Ukraine not only with rhetoric but with the armaments and aid necessary for triumph. Because this is not merely Ukraine’s battle—it is a crusade for the very essence of liberty, democracy, and human dignity.

Slava Ukraini. The world must not falter.
